#  Introduction

::: {.callout-note}

This report reflects on my learning experience with RevealJS presentations and advanced data wrangling in R. The report demonstrates both technical skills and personal reflections gained throughout Module 6.

:::

## Prompt

\*\* In Step 1, you learned how to design stunning presentation slides with Quarto. What's your impression of the RevealJS presentation? Describe its capabilities as you learned from the presentations. What are its strengths and weaknesses compared with PPT?\*\*

## Response

RevealJS was one of the most interesting tools I learned during this course. It allows users to create presentations using Quarto and Markdown rather than designing slides manually. The presentation is generated from code, which makes it highly reproducible and easy to update.

Some capabilities of RevealJS include:

- Interactive slides

- Navigation controls

- Embedded code

- Tables and charts

- Incremental bullet points

- Themes and custom styling

- Publication to GitHub Pages

Compared with Microsoft PowerPoint, RevealJS offers better reproducibility and integration with data analysis workflows. Since slides are generated directly from code, any changes in the data can automatically update the presentation.

However, RevealJS also has weaknesses. PowerPoint provides a more user-friendly drag-and-drop interface and offers more visual editing tools. Beginners may find RevealJS difficult because it requires familiarity with Markdown and coding concepts.

Overall, I believe RevealJS is powerful for data analysts because it combines presentation design with reproducible research.

## Strengths and Weaknesses

\| Strengths of RevealJS \| Weaknesses of RevealJS \|

\|----------\|----------\|

\| Reproducible \| Requires coding \|

\| Works with Quarto \| Steeper learning curve \|

\| Easy web publishing \| Less intuitive design tools \|

\| Integrates with R \| More setup required \|

# Example Reproducible Chart

\`\`\`{r}

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars,

aes(x = wt,

y = mpg)) +

geom_point(color = "blue") +

labs(

title = "Vehicle Weight vs MPG",

x = "Weight",

y = "Miles Per Gallon"

)

\`\`\`

Figure \@fig-weight demonstrates the relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency.

# Advanced Data Wrangling

## Prompt

\*\*My advanced wrangling lecture in Step 3 introduced new concepts, including how to join relational databases. Pick three different functions, each from a different category. Describe when to use them and give one coding example along with an output for each function.\*\*

# Function 1: left_join()

## When to Use

The \`left_join()\` function is used when we want to keep all records from the left table and bring matching information from another table.

\`\`\`{r}

library(dplyr)

students \<- data.frame(

id = c(1,2,3),

name = c("Amy","Bob","Chris")

)

grades \<- data.frame

id = c(1,2),

grade = c("A","B")

)

left_join(students, grades, by = "id")

\`\`\`

### Output Discussion

The output keeps all students. If no matching grade exists, the result displays NA.

# Function 2: filter()

## When to Use

The \`filter()\` function is used to select rows that satisfy a specific condition.

\`\`\`{r}

library(dplyr)

filter(mtcars, mpg \> 25)

\`\`\`

### Output Discussion

This output displays only vehicles that achieve more than 25 miles per gallon.

# Function 3: summarize()

## When to Use

The \`summarize()\` function is useful for calculating statistics such as averages, totals, counts, minimums, and maximums.

\`\`\`{r}

library(dplyr)

mtcars %\>%

summarize(

Average_MPG = mean(mpg)

)

\`\`\`

### Output Discussion

The function calculates the average miles per gallon across all vehicles in the dataset.
